title: Sworn Instead
logline: A small walled temple on a misty hill shoulder, whose name means the place of the oath, where a quarrel that would otherwise have ended in a blow ends instead in one sentence said out loud under an enormous tree — and the legal system is reported to accept the sentence.
human_question: If I had to climb a hill and say out loud, in a place built for nothing else, that what I am claiming is true, would I still be claiming it?

place.what_kind_of_place: A small walled temple compound on a shoulder of hill country about a thousand metres up, at the edge of a plateau of vegetable plots and wet green slopes. Inside the wall there is one tree very much larger than anything else in sight — a bo tree grown from a cutting of the island's oldest documented planted tree — with a small brick dagoba standing in under its canopy, an image house, a rail, a lamp and a stretch of swept earth. It is a Buddhist temple in daily use, and it is also visited by Hindu pilgrims, because tradition holds this to be the ground where Sita walked into fire to prove her word; figures and painted panels of Rama, Sita and Hanuman stand a few metres from the Buddha images. The whole compound could be crossed in twenty paces. The thing that makes it a place at all is not its architecture but its name, which means the place of the oath, and the arrangement that name describes: for a very long time this has been regarded as the proper ground on which to swear, out loud, when a quarrel has to be settled. It is the smallest and the quietest location in this group, and the only one whose subject is a form of words.
place.why_it_is_worth_watching: Four things carry it with the sound off, and none of them is big. The light: an enormous canopy over a small space, so that at the middle of a grey day everything under the tree is green, and the green moves. The weather: hill mist coming over a low wall and filling the compound, then thinning and going, on a cycle of a few minutes, all morning. The surfaces: brick furred with lichen, roots crossing swept earth, wet leaf litter, a rag of cloth on a rail, the paint of new figures beside the plaster of old ones — a film that can be shot almost entirely at close range and at macro. And emptiness: a frame with a huge tree in it and nobody under it, held long enough that the viewer starts listening instead of looking. There is no aerial, no reveal and almost no camera movement anywhere in it.
place.what_moves_or_changes: Only weather and light, and nothing at all is arranged. Mist crosses the wall and clears. Rain comes onto the canopy and comes off it a drop at a time for an hour after it has stopped. The green under the tree changes every time the cloud opens. In the evening the lamp is the brightest thing in the frame and the sky is the second. Nothing is opened, lit, wound, carried or done for the camera, because the film's subject is an arrangement rather than an event, and the arrangement is not a thing you can watch — it is a sentence, and the film never films one.
place.when_it_looks_best: Overcast hill mornings, which is most mornings: a flat grey sky is what makes the light under the canopy green rather than blotchy, and hard high sun is the one condition that ruins the film. The mist is best in the first two or three hours after dawn. The wet months give rain on leaves, water coming off the canopy and saturated colour in the brick and the moss. Late afternoon gives the one warm frame the film is allowed, through the canopy from the west, and then the compound going blue with a single lamp in it.

two_layers.without_the_philosophy: A quiet film about one very small place in hill weather. Mist filling a walled yard at dawn and leaving it; a canopy so large that the space beneath it has its own light; rain coming off leaves; brick, lichen, roots and swept earth at close range; two sets of sacred images standing a few metres apart; and then the stillest frame in the series, a patch of empty ground held for a long time while the light changes on it. It resolves on its own terms — grey to green to gold to blue, wide-ish to macro, weather arriving and going — and someone who never hears a word of the narration gets a complete, unhurried piece with a beginning, a middle and a payoff that is intimate rather than grand. It is the smallest film here on purpose, and it is the only one with nothing happening in it.
two_layers.with_the_philosophy: The same footage becomes a demonstration, because this place is an institution built for one precise moment: the moment two people want to strike each other. The voice does not moralise and does not read anybody's mind; it explains what the ground is for. The books say that the states rooted in aversion never arrive without a painful feeling of their own, so the person holding one is the first to pay for it. They list the ordinary occasions, and the occasions are a boundary, a debt, a word not accepted, a thing asked for and not given. They name, among the fourteen unwholesome factors, exactly the items a quarrel over ground is made of — not bearing that a thing of yours should be another's, be of use to another, be equalled by another, or even be known about — and they file every one of them with aversion rather than with wanting. And they list, among the causes of the state, not thinking the thing through. What this hill supplies is the thinking-through, built as an object: a climb, a wait, a tree, and a sentence said out loud in a place whose name is the saying of it.

sequence.on_screen: First light, from below, camera on a tripod and never moving: green hill country under moving mist, and inside a low compound wall one tree far larger than anything else in the frame. The mist crosses the wall, fills the yard, thins and goes.
sequence.voice: The name of this place means the place of the oath. People have been coming up here for a very long time to say one thing out loud, because saying it here is supposed to settle a quarrel. The books this series is reading count exactly two states of mind rooted in aversion, and they are firm about one thing before anything else: neither of them ever arrives without a painful feeling of its own.

sequence.on_screen: Under the canopy, looking straight up, held for a long time. Green light, a lattice of leaves, water coming off them one drop at a time. Ambient sound only — leaves, water, one bird, a road a long way off.
sequence.voice: The definition they give is plain. Something disliked is met, and the mind strikes against it and wants it gone. One of the two texts explains the word for it as striking against the thing. Whoever has it is carrying it first, before anyone else is touched. And the same books say, in the same breath, that this is where harm to other people begins — so none of this should be heard as the comfortable idea that anger only hurts the angry.

sequence.on_screen: Close and static, then macro: the brick of a small dagoba standing in under the tree, lichen on it, roots crossing swept earth, a rail, an oil lamp, a rag of cloth tied on. Shallow focus, available light, no camera movement.
sequence.voice: The occasions the texts actually list are not battles. Your word was not accepted. What you asked for was not given. Somebody handled a thing you look after. You remembered something that was done to you. That is a fence in the wrong place, or a debt, or a strip of ground two families both count as theirs. It is what people walk up a hill about.

sequence.on_screen: Two held frames cut together, neither wider nor longer than the other, neither first by more than an edit. Buddha images in the image house. A few metres away, figures and painted panels of Rama, Sita and Hanuman. Available light, nobody in frame.
sequence.voice: Tradition holds this to be the ground where Sita walked into fire to prove that her word was true. Hindu pilgrims come here for that; Buddhist devotees come for the tree and the shrine. Whether it happened, and whether it happened here, this film does not settle and has no way to. What the two accounts have in common is the problem the whole place is arranged around: a word that somebody else has to be able to believe. The second list these films use names fourteen unwholesome factors, and says four of them are present in every single unwholesome moment. One of the four is having no dread at all of doing wrong.

sequence.on_screen: The lane up, at eye level on a long lens: wet tarmac, a gate, steps, a noticeboard, mist closing the far end, nobody on it. Then the empty compound in rain, one locked-off frame held for a minute.
sequence.voice: Here is the arrangement, as far as it can be established. Two people in a quarrel come up. One of them says out loud, in this place, that what they are claiming is true, and that is reported to be accepted when the quarrel is settled. Who administers it, and by what authority, this film does not claim to know. What the older text names among the causes of this state of mind is simply not thinking the thing through — and almost everything about this arrangement is the time that takes.

sequence.on_screen: The tree from the far side of the compound through mist, long lens, flattened and nearly monochrome. Then rain on the canopy, held. Nothing enters either frame.
sequence.voice: The list of fourteen is worth hearing item by item, because part of it is a description of what a quarrel over ground is made of. Not bearing that a thing of yours should belong to somebody else. Not bearing that somebody else should get any use from it. Not bearing that somebody else should have one as good. Not bearing that anyone should even know what you have. The first of the five kinds counted there is about the place a person lives. And facing the other way, there is not bearing somebody else's good fortune. Neither of those is filed with wanting. Both are filed with aversion.

sequence.on_screen: The stillest frame in the film: swept ground under the canopy, empty, mist, one leaf turning over on the earth. Held until it is slightly uncomfortable. No music at any point.
sequence.voice: The worst case in these books is exact. A person wants something, a living thing is in the way, and the wish turns into remove it. What this hill puts into that space is a form of words. And there is no discount for being in the right: one of the texts says that the hatred felt towards someone who really has come to harm you is the fiercest form of the same thing, not a better kind of it. The ground is empty because saying a sentence takes up almost no room.

sequence.on_screen: Late light through the canopy, one static frame. Then the compound as the light goes, the lamp the brightest thing left and the sky the second. Ambient only. The film ends close on the tree, not wide.
sequence.voice: And afterwards, nothing. The texts are unusually blunt here: going over a wrong again and again does not thin it out, it makes a light one heavy. Remembering is not the fault; churning is. Whatever was said here today was said once, out loud, in a place whose name is the saying of it, and then two people walked back down a hill. That is the entire institution. It is almost nothing — and it is standing exactly where a blow would have been.

concept_merge.why_together: C007 supplies the event the place exists for, and C022 supplies its contents. Read fresh, C007 is a claim about cost and a list of occasions. Both hate-rooted minds are always accompanied by a painful mental feeling and by aversion, and they differ only in whether they arise spontaneously or after urging [C007-P:L25–L28; C007-M:L3–L9]; the definition is that a disliked object is met and the mind strikes against it and wants it destroyed [C007-P:L32–L34], which Margaya explains through the name paṭigha, striking against the object [C007-M:L3]. Then the occasions, and they are startlingly domestic: one's word not accepted, a thing asked for and not given, others handling something one looks after, a past hostility recalled [C007-M:L17], alongside Pradeepika's standing afflictions including not getting what one wants [C007-P:L49]. That is the docket of a village quarrel, and Pradeepika also lists among the causes of the state simply not thinking the object through [C007-P:L45] — which is the one cause an institution can actually do something about. C022 then names, in the sources' own words, what the quarrel is made of. Four of the fourteen factors are present in every unwholesome moment, and one of them is having no dread of wrongdoing [C022-P:L31; C022-M:L3; C022-P:L63], which is precisely the thing an oath is constructed to restore; Pradeepika calls shamelessness and that absence of dread the two great forces without which no unwholesome act can be done at all [C022-P:L69]. And its account of stinginess is not a generality but an inventory: not bearing that a thing of one's own should belong to another, be of use to another, be equalled by another, or even be known about [C022-P:L133], with dwelling the first of the five kinds counted [C022-P:L135; C022-M:L45]; facing outward, envy cannot bear another's prosperity [C022-P:L129]; and both are filed with aversion rather than with wanting [C022-P:L121]. On a hill whose name means the place of the oath, those two digests stop being lists and become a description of what happens twenty paces from the camera without anybody being filmed.
concept_merge.what_it_reveals: That the sources are not describing a moral failing but a mechanism with a gap in it, and that this place is a two-thousand-year-old attempt to put something in the gap. C007 alone would send the film hunting for an angry person, which this location forbids absolutely and which the digests forbid anyway. C022 alone would be an inventory with nothing at stake. Together they make the argument the place already is: the state costs the holder first, its occasions are a boundary and a debt, one of its named causes is not thinking the matter through, and one of the four constants in every unwholesome moment is the absence of dread at doing wrong. An institution that answers all four at once would be a climb, a delay, and a sentence a person has to say out loud somewhere that makes them afraid to say it falsely. That is what is on the hill. The film's payoff is therefore not a spectacle but an absence: a patch of empty swept ground, held, where a blow would have been.

concept_links.why: The digest carries every load this film puts on it. Both hate-rooted minds always arise with a painful mental feeling and with aversion, splitting only on whether they are spontaneous or prompted [C007-P:L25–L28; C007-M:L3–L9], so the film's first claim — that whoever holds this carries it first — is the sources' own and not an inspirational gloss. The definition supplies the moment the place is built for: a disagreeable, unwanted object is met, and because it is felt as hostile the mind wants to destroy it [C007-P:L32–L34], which Margaya names as striking against the object [C007-M:L3]. The occasions are what make this a film about a boundary rather than about rage: one's word not accepted, a thing asked for and refused, another handling what one looks after, a past hostility remembered [C007-M:L17], together with Pradeepika's not getting what one wants [C007-P:L49]. Pradeepika's list of causes gives the film its hinge, because one of them is not thinking the object through [C007-P:L45]; the arrangement on this hill is made almost entirely of the delay that thinking requires. Beat 7 uses Pradeepika's hardest example — a wish that turns into removing a living obstacle [C007-P:L59] — only to name what stands in that space here instead, and never to suggest that anybody who comes here wanted to kill anybody. Four digest limits are load-bearing and are honoured in the beats. There is no exception for righteous anger: Margaya says the hatred felt when killing an enemy who has come to harm you is the fierce form of the same state [C007-M:L11], which beat 7 states outright, because a dispute film with a wronged party in it invites exactly that exemption. The slogan that anger only hurts yourself is refused in beat 2, because the sources also say plainly that this state leads to killing and harming others [C007-P:L47; C007-P:L53]. The bodily effects Pradeepika describes and its claim about such minds at the time of death are traditional teaching and are never narrated as observable fact [C007-P:L47; C007-P:L51]; only the clause that right and wrong stop being visible is used, and it is attributed to the text. And L44's cause, which the digest flags as unclear and needing expert reading, is not used at all.

Three things are taken from this digest and nothing else is. First, the four factors present in every one of the twelve unwholesome minds, among them having no dread of the consequences of wrongdoing [C022-P:L31; C022-M:L3; C022-P:L63], with Pradeepika naming shamelessness and that absence together as the two great forces without which no unwholesome act can be done [C022-P:L69]. That is the single most useful sentence in the group for this location, because an oath is a device for putting dread of doing wrong back in front of a person, and beat 4 says so without claiming it works. Second, the precise inventory of stinginess: not bearing that something of one's own should belong to another, should be of use to another, should be matched by another's, or should even be known about [C022-P:L133], counted in five kinds of which the first is dwelling [C022-P:L135; C022-M:L45] — a boundary quarrel is exactly that item, and it is named, so the film does not have to reach. Third, envy facing the other way, unable to bear another's prosperity [C022-P:L129], and the placement that surprises everybody: both are filed with aversion, not with wanting, and Pradeepika lists revenge and the wish to destroy among aversion's forms [C022-P:L121]. Beat 8 uses the digest's account of remorse, which says that brooding over a wrong makes a light one heavy and that recalling it is not itself the fault [C022-P:L141; C022-P:L143]. The digest's exclusions shape what is left out. Conceit is not used at all, because the digest warns that 'I am inferior' is classed here as conceit and must never be turned on real disadvantage [C022-P:L111; C022-M:L31], and that Pradeepika's equal-conceit description contains egalitarian-sounding sentences which would badly mislead if quoted near people arguing for a fair share [C022-P:L109]. Doubt is not used, because the digest says ordinary uncertainty about unknown matters is not the doubt meant [C022-P:L179; C022-M:L57] — which matters in a film about a place where what is at issue is whose account is true. Remorse is never presented as purifying, which the digest explicitly rejects [C022-P:L143], so the film does not let the oath read as an absolution. And the moth-and-lamp image is not used, because it belongs to the source's illustration of fearlessness of wrongdoing [C022-P:L67] and would read here as a picture of the people who come.

what_the_viewer_could_understand: That aversion is not first a harm done to somebody else but a cost paid by whoever is holding it, and that the occasions the texts actually list for it are a fence, a debt and a word not taken seriously. That the old inventory of what a quarrel is made of is startlingly exact — not bearing that a thing of mine should be yours, or be of use to you, or be matched by yours, or even be known to you — and that all of it is classed as displeasure rather than as appetite. And that somebody, a very long time ago, drew the obvious conclusion and built for it: if one of the causes is not thinking the thing through, then make people climb, and wait, and say it out loud where saying it falsely frightens them. The viewer is left with what that costs and what it replaces, and with no verdict about anyone's quarrel, because the film never sees one.
what_must_be_real: Binding, and it governs the whole film: no oath is filmed, and nobody in a dispute is filmed. Whoever comes to this place to swear is doing so about a real quarrel with real stakes and real consequences after the film is finished, is identifiable to their own village, and cannot meaningfully consent to being part of a documentary about it. No party, no opposing party, no witness, no relative, no official, no monk administering anything, no ceremony and no words spoken in the course of settling a quarrel. Not staged, not re-enacted, not reconstructed with stand-ins, not overheard, and not 'observed discreetly' — the discreet version is the worst version, because it removes even the possibility of refusal. No beat in this film depends on any of it: the film is the place, the weather and the arrangement, and the voice is what explains what happens here. Beyond that: the tree, the shrine, the two sets of images, the mist and the condition of the compound are filmed as they are; no act of worship is interrupted, restarted, re-lit or asked for again, and no devotee of either tradition is filmed identifiably or presented as an example of anything. Neither tradition on this ground is ranked, corrected, dated against the other or described as borrowing from the other; the epic identification is said to be tradition, which is what it is, and the film does not adjudicate whether or where those events happened. The drone stays on the ground: at a small living shrine it is treated as refused, and every frame in the film is obtainable on foot from inside or just outside the wall.
position_hint: late in the group, and the quietest thing in it: it is the film that asks what could possibly be done about the state the other films have been showing, and the answer only lands once the cost has been established. It also wants to follow the group's loudest and largest films so that the drop in scale is felt. No location reasoning is involved.
risks: Any drift towards filming a real dispute or a real oath, in any form, including a 'generic' oath filmed with willing participants — willing participants in a real quarrel are still parties to it, and the film has no way to protect them afterwards.

Moralising about litigation, or letting the voice imply that swearing is better, purer or more honest than going to court; the film describes an arrangement and makes no recommendation about how anyone should settle anything.
Treating the practice as quaint local colour, folklore or a curiosity for visitors. It is a working arrangement about money, land and reputation, and the register of the narration has to match that.

Ranking the two traditions that share the ground, dating one against the other, presenting either as derivative, or stating the epic identification as established history; it is tradition and the film says so. Note also that the archaeological literature flatly denies the identification and says the Hindu figures and paintings were added recently — the film records that this is contested and takes no side about whose ground it is.
Letting the source's remorse material read as absolution, as if the oath cleaned something; the digest explicitly rejects the idea that brooding regret purifies [C022-P:L143].
Narrating the traditional bodily effects of aversion, or the claim about such minds at the time of death, as observable or medical fact [C007-P:L47; C007-P:L51].
The righteous-anger exemption, which a film about a boundary dispute invites more strongly than almost any other subject; the sources make no exception for anger at a real wrong [C007-M:L11].

Importing conceit into the film, especially the source's 'I am inferior' form or its equal-conceit description, in a place where people come because they believe they have been wronged; the digest rules both out of this territory [C022-P:L109; C022-P:L111].
Filming at a small living shrine as if it were a monument: crowding a compound twenty paces across with a crew, or lighting anything, changes the only thing the film has, which is stillness.
Flying a drone here at all. It is treated as refused, and a film that needs an aerial to work is the wrong film for this place.
drop_if: The film cannot be made without filming an oath, a party to a dispute, or a ceremony — in which case it is not made.
The incumbent of the temple does not want the arrangement discussed on camera, or wants it discussed only in terms the film cannot honestly use.
The practice turns out not to exist in any current form and to be entirely a construction of tourism copy, in which case the film has no subject and the record says so rather than filming the copy.
Filming cannot happen without interrupting worship in a compound this small, or without devotees of either tradition being identifiable.
The site's recent alterations have gone far enough that the place can only be filmed as a themed attraction, which is a different and much worse film.

connections.note: This record formerly carried a water-allocation film — a great restored tank opened on a decided day, the water running out along a channel until it stopped. IDEA-0041 is the same film and the more specific of the two: one reservoir's water released on a written rotation, with every gate and painted gauge a decision about whose fields get it. Two water-allocation films in a group of nine was a duplicate, and rather than merge places two hundred kilometres apart that share only a mechanism, the weaker one was dropped outright and this record rebuilt on a different subject. IDEA-0041 keeps the water.
Two boundaries and two remedies: one drawn between people and animals, where nothing can be said to the other side at all, and one drawn between neighbours, where the entire remedy is something said.
Two arrangements agreed in advance so that two parties who both have a claim on the same thing do not meet head-on: one worked out in hardware on a line, one worked out in a form of words on a hill.

selection.reason: The record is kept and the film on it replaced. Its previous film duplicated IDEA-0041, which does the same water-allocation argument more specifically; the replacement buys the group a tradition it did not have (a shared Buddhist and Hindu site), a district it did not have, and the treatment it was missing — the small, still, ground-only film with no drone and no event in it. It is also the only film in the group whose subject is a form of words rather than a thing.

review.note: Body rewritten in full on 2026-09-25, so any earlier verdict on this record refers to a film that no longer exists. The previous film, a great tank opened on a decided day with the water running out along a channel until it stopped, was dropped outright because IDEA-0041 in this same group is the same film and the more specific of the two — one reservoir's water let out on a written rotation, with every gate and gauge a decision about whose fields get water and whose wait. Two water-allocation films in a group of nine is a duplicate; the two places are two hundred kilometres apart and share only a mechanism, so a merge would have said nothing, and replacing this one outright is what buys the group its differentiation. The replacement is a small hill temple whose name means the place of the oath, and the film is built on a verified historical binding: the site has long been regarded as the proper ground on which to swear when a quarrel is being settled, an oath sworn here is reported to be permitted and accepted when disputes are settled, it is also held by tradition to be where Sita underwent the fire ordeal and is venerated by Buddhist and Hindu devotees alike, and the archaeological record attributes the temple to Aggabodhi IV in the seventh century, with a sapling of the great Bodhi tree of the old capital planted here, a small dagoba later built beneath it, a fragmentary slab inscription of Mahinda IV found at the old Bodhi tree premises, and the stupa and Bodhi pedestal gazetted as protected monuments in 2002 and 2008. Whether the legal recognition is statutory or customary could not be established and is recorded in what_is_disputed, not asserted; so is the fact that the archaeological literature denies the epic identification outright and says the Hindu figures and paintings were added recently. A separate temple in another district, which holds an actual swearing stone and the royal-court and cobra folklore of one of the later kingdoms, is routinely conflated with this one in search results and travel copy, and that conflation is recorded and excluded. Both concept links were re-tested against the digests and rewritten: C007 is now carried by its own list of everyday occasions and, decisively, by the cause it names as not thinking the object through, which is what the arrangement on this hill is made of; C022 is narrowed to the four constants and the absence of dread at wrongdoing, the exact inventory of stinginess with dwelling among its five kinds, envy facing outward, and the refusal to let remorse read as purification — with conceit and doubt dropped entirely because the digest rules both out of this territory. The hardest constraint is written into what_must_be_real as binding: no oath and no party to a dispute is filmed, in any form, staged or observed, and no beat depends on one. New title; the old title is kept in aliases. Treatment is the group's quiet film — ground only, no drone, almost no camera movement, ambient sound, an intimate payoff. Commons holds nothing honest for this site, so images is empty and the research note says so.

suggested_location.region: Badulla District, Uva Province: at Nugatalawa, about 4 km west of Welimada town on the Nuwara Eliya–Badulla road, on the Welimada plateau in the eastern hill country. Several tourism pages place it in the Central Province; that appears to be wrong. Welimada is in the Badulla District of the Uva Province, and the heritage literature that records the gazetted monuments gives Badulla District. The error is easy to see the cause of: the site is on the road in from Nuwara Eliya, which is in the Central Province, and is marketed on a trail run out of Nuwara Eliya.
suggested_location.why_here: Because the concept and the picture are the same object here, and the object is a word. This is the only candidate found anywhere in the slate where an institution exists for the exact moment C007 describes — a disliked object met, the mind striking against it, wanting it gone — and where the institution's answer is not force, not a judge and not a payment, but a sentence said out loud in a named place. The name is the argument: it means the place of the oath, and the practice the name records is that this is where you come when a quarrel has to be settled. C007 lists among the causes of that state of mind not thinking the matter through, and this arrangement is made almost entirely of the interval that thinking takes: a road, a climb, a gate, a wait, a tree. C022 then supplies the contents, and they are not approximations — the inventory of what a person cannot bear about their own things, with dwelling first among its five kinds, is a description of a boundary quarrel written down more than a thousand years before the quarrel. Cinematically it earns its place by being the opposite of everything else in the group: a compound twenty paces across, one enormous canopy making its own green light, mist crossing a low wall all morning, rain coming off leaves for an hour after the rain stops, brick and lichen and swept earth at macro range, two sets of sacred images standing a few metres apart, and one held frame of empty ground as the payoff. It needs no aerial, no reveal and almost no camera movement, which is precisely the treatment this group has nowhere else. It also fixes two differentiation problems at once: it is the group's only shared Buddhist and Hindu site, and its only film set at altitude in the hill country.

historical_thread.story:
The place is named for what is done there. Divurumpola means the place of the oath in Sinhala, and the temple's long-standing reputation is as the proper ground on which to swear when a quarrel is being settled between parties. The formula that recurs across the Sri Lankan and Indian travel and heritage literature is that the legal system permits and accepts the swearing done at this temple while settling disputes between parties, that villagers still take oaths there, and that in certain courts the resulting agreement was binding; several versions add that an oath taken here remains valid before village courts or grama sabhas, and that a great many disputes are still settled at the site. What could not be found behind that formula, in any search made for this record, is a statute, a section of the Oaths and Affirmations Ordinance, a reported case, or any official document naming this place. The Oaths Ordinance consolidates the law of oaths and affirmations in judicial proceedings and provides for affirmation in place of an oath for those who object to swearing, but nothing located in it or in any secondary account attaches legal effect to a particular temple. The colonial-period comparative literature does record the local accommodation of customary oath forms — swearing at a devale, and in some communities at a mosque — as a recognised practice in Dutch Ceylon, which makes a customary rather than statutory basis by far the likelier reading; but that is an inference, not a source about this place, and it is recorded here as unresolved.

The archaeological record is separate from the practice and is much firmer. The temple's founding is attributed to Aggabodhi IV, king of Anuradhapura, whose reign is given as 673 to 689 CE. A sapling of the Anuradhapura Bodhi tree is recorded as having been planted here as a mark of respect, and a small dagoba was built subsequently beneath that tree. The ancient monuments identifiable on the premises are the small stupa, the Bodhi tree and the image house. A fragmentary slab inscription of the reign of Mahinda IV (956–972 CE) was found at the old Bodhi tree premises; it is a medieval Sinhala record of immunities granted in respect of some land belonging to a vihara. The ancient stupa and the Bodhi pedestal were declared protected archaeological monuments by government gazette notifications published on 22 November 2002 and 6 June 2008. The old paintings in the image house were covered in 1983 when new paintings were drawn over them.

The third layer is the epic one, and it is the one that now brings most visitors. Tradition holds this to be the place where Sita, rescued from Ravana, underwent the Agni Pariksha — the fire ordeal — to prove her chastity to Rama, entering the pyre and emerging unharmed. On the Ramayana trail run through the hill country the site is ranked immediately after Sita Eliya and Ashok Vatika in importance, and it draws pilgrims from India as well as Sri Lankan Hindu devotees. Sculptures of Rama, Sita and Hanuman stand in the compound alongside the Buddha images, and Ramayana paintings have been added to the temple. The identification is disputed at the root: the Sri Lankan heritage literature states flatly that there is no archaeological or historical evidence for it, that the temple is being promoted as a Hindu Rama-and-Sita place by some locals and tourist agencies, and that the new Hindu figures and paintings were created recently by the temple authorities to encourage that reading. The obvious hinge of the identification is the name itself: a place called the place of the oath is an inviting home for a story about a woman who had to prove her word.

One confusion has to be held off, because it contaminates almost every search made on this subject. A different temple, Divurum Bodhi Viharaya at Ampitiya in the Kandy District of the Central Province — a Ramanya Nikaya temple established in 1914 — holds the Divurum Gala, a swearing stone engraved with a sun and a moon and said to date from the Dambadeniya period, and carries the tradition that during the Kingdom of Kandy the kings used part of its ground as a court, where an accused person swore innocence by touching the stone, and that Kandyan folklore held a false swearer would be killed by a cobra within three days. That is a rich and filmable story and it belongs to that temple, not to this one. Nothing in it is used here, and the two sites are recorded as distinct.
historical_thread.how_it_binds:
The digests do not resemble this place; they describe what it is for.

C007's account runs in four steps, and the arrangement on this hill answers each of them. Step one: a disagreeable, unwanted object is met, and because it is felt as hostile the mind wants to destroy it, which the sources name as striking against the object. Step two: this never arrives without a painful mental feeling, in either of the two forms — so the first person harmed is the person holding it. Step three, and this is where the place stops being an analogy: the occasions the texts list are not rage or war, they are one's word not accepted, a thing asked for and not given, another person handling something one looks after, and a past hostility remembered. That is not a description of a battlefield; it is a description of the docket at a village boundary. Step four is the causal list, and it contains the item the whole institution turns on — among the main conditions for the state arising is not thinking the object through. That is the one cause in the list that is addressable from outside a person's mind. You cannot legislate away a disliked object and you cannot abolish displeasure, but you can insert an interval between the object and the act, and you can make the interval expensive. A road, a climb, a gate, a wait, a tree and a sentence said out loud is an interval, physically built, at the scale of an afternoon.

C022 supplies the inventory, and its precision is what makes the binding tight rather than suggestive. The sources count fourteen unwholesome factors and say four of them are present in every unwholesome mind whatever else is there, one of the four being having no dread at all of the consequences of wrongdoing; Pradeepika calls shamelessness and that absence together the two great forces without which no unwholesome act is possible. An oath is a technology for reinstating exactly that dread — not a punishment, not a proof, but a device that makes a person afraid of their own sentence. Whether it works is not a claim this film makes; that it is aimed at that named factor is legible in the arrangement. Then the contents of the quarrel. Pradeepika's stinginess is four unbearables, listed: that something of one's own should belong to another, that another should get use of it, that another should have one to match, that anyone should even know of it — and the first of the five kinds counted is about dwelling, about the place one lives. A boundary dispute is not like that list. It is on that list. Envy is its mirror, facing outward, unable to bear another's prosperity. And the classification that would surprise most viewers is the one that makes the place coherent: both are filed with aversion rather than with wanting, which means the texts already regard the person clutching a strip of ground as being in pain rather than in enjoyment. Aversion's own named forms include the intention of revenge and the wish to destroy.

Put the two together and the site reads as an institution built where the mechanism has its gap. The state costs the holder first. Its occasions are a fence and a debt. Its named contents are precisely what two neighbours are arguing about. One of its causes is haste. One of the four constants in every unwholesome moment is the missing dread of doing wrong. And on a hill somebody built, out of a road, a tree, a name and a sentence, an answer that addresses haste and dread at the same time and leaves the deciding to the parties. It is worth saying what the binding does not claim. It does not claim the arrangement is superior to a court, or that swearing is more honest than litigating; the sources say nothing whatever about legal systems. It does not claim anybody who comes here is angry, envious or grasping, which no camera can see and which the digests forbid asserting. And the epic layer is not adjudicated: the film notes that two traditions share the ground and that both are about a word somebody else has to be able to believe, which is true of the story and true of the practice, and it goes no further than that.
what_is_certain: Divurumpola means the place of the oath in Sinhala. The name is the site's own and is the reason both the practice and the epic identification attach to it.

The temple is at Nugatalawa, about 4 km from Welimada town, on the Nuwara Eliya–Badulla road, reached by a turnoff reported near the 96th kilometre post and about 20 km from Nuwara Eliya. Welimada is in the Badulla District of the Uva Province.

The temple has long been regarded as a suitable place for oaths taken in settling disputes between parties; this is the consistent report of every source consulted, Sri Lankan and foreign, heritage and commercial.
The founding of the temple is attributed to King Aggabodhi IV, king of Anuradhapura, whose reign is given as 673–689 CE.
A sapling of the Anuradhapura Bodhi tree is recorded as having been planted here as a mark of respect, and a small dagoba was built subsequently beneath that tree.
The ancient monuments identifiable at the site are the small stupa, the Bodhi tree and the image house.

A fragmentary slab inscription of the reign of King Mahinda IV (956–972 CE) was found at the old Bodhi tree premises. It is a medieval Sinhala record of immunities granted in respect of some land belonging to a vihara.
The ancient stupa and the Bodhi pedestal were declared protected archaeological monuments by government gazette notifications published on 22 November 2002 and 6 June 2008.
The old paintings in the image house were covered in 1983 by new paintings drawn over them.

The site is on the Ramayana trail, is described as ranking immediately after Sita Eliya and Ashok Vatika among the island's Ramayana pilgrimage sites, and is visited by Hindu pilgrims from India as well as by Sri Lankan devotees. Sculptures of Rama, Sita and Hanuman stand in the compound alongside Buddha images, and Ramayana paintings have been added to the temple.

Reported visiting arrangements: open daily 06:00 to 20:00, with an entrance charge of about 500 Sri Lankan rupees for foreign visitors and a published telephone number for the temple. These are from commercial listings and may be out of date.

Divurum Bodhi Viharaya at Ampitiya, Kandy District, Central Province, is a different temple: a Ramanya Nikaya temple established in 1914, holding the Divurum Gala swearing stone engraved with a sun and a moon and said to date from the Dambadeniya period, together with the tradition of Kandyan kings using its ground as a court and the folklore that a false swearer is killed by a cobra within three days. None of that belongs to the site proposed here.
what_is_disputed: Above all, the status of the legal recognition, which could not be established. The claim that the legal system permits and accepts an oath sworn at this temple when parties are settling a dispute, and that such an oath is still valid before village courts or grama sabhas, is repeated almost word for word across dozens of pages, all of which appear to descend from one or two common sources. No statute, no section of the Oaths and Affirmations Ordinance, no reported case and no official document naming this place was located. The Oaths Ordinance consolidates the law of oaths and affirmations in judicial proceedings and provides for affirmation in place of an oath; nothing found in it attaches effect to a named place. Whether the recognition is statutory, whether it is a customary practice that the courts and mediation boards accommodate in fact, or whether it is a well-worn piece of tourism copy repeated until it sounds official, is unresolved. It is the single most important thing to settle before this film is made, it is a question for a Sri Lankan lawyer rather than for search, and the film's narration is written so that it does not depend on the answer: beat 5 says the practice is reported to be accepted and says outright that who administers it and by what authority is not known here.

How the oath is actually administered — who is present, what is said, whether it is sworn before the Bodhi tree, the stupa or the image house, whether a monk or a village official officiates, whether anything is written down, and whether the two parties come together or separately. No first-hand account of the procedure at this site was found in any language searched.

Whether it is still used, and how often. Sources say only that villagers 'still' take oaths there and that 'lots of disputes' are settled; no figure, register, year or named case was found, and nothing distinguishes an active practice from a remembered one.

The Ramayana identification, which is disputed at the root rather than at the edges. Tradition holds this to be the site of Sita's fire ordeal, and it is a living object of Hindu devotion; the Sri Lankan heritage literature states flatly that there is no archaeological or historical evidence for it, that the identification is promoted by some locals and tourist agencies, and that the Hindu figures and Ramayana paintings were created recently by the temple authorities to encourage that reading. Both of those are recorded, neither is settled here, and the film does not adjudicate whether the events of the epic happened or where. The name is the plain hinge: a place called the place of the oath is a natural home for a story about a woman who had to prove her word.

The province. Several tourism and travel pages place the temple in the Central Province. Welimada is in the Badulla District of the Uva Province and the heritage literature giving the gazetted monuments places the temple in the Badulla District. Uva is used here and the discrepancy is recorded rather than silently corrected.

The date and lineage of the tree. A sapling of the Anuradhapura Bodhi tree is what the sources say was planted; whether the tree standing today is that tree, a successor, or a later planting is not established anywhere, and no girth, age estimate or measurement was found. The film's central image is a large tree; no claim about its age appears in the narration.

The attribution to Aggabodhi IV. It is the standard attribution in the heritage literature; no chronicle passage or inscription supporting it was checked in this research, and seventh-century foundation attributions for hill-country temples are frequently traditional rather than documented.

The relationship between this site's oath practice and the Kandy-district swearing stone. Search engines, travel copy and at least one summary merge the two, transferring the Divurum Gala, the Kandyan court and the cobra folklore onto this temple. Nothing found establishes that this site has a swearing stone, a court tradition or a cobra story of its own. They are treated as separate sites here, and the fact that the conflation is widespread is itself the finding.

what_to_film: The compound from below at first light, on a tripod, not moving: hill country under mist, a low wall, and one tree far larger than anything else in frame. The same set-up held long enough to catch mist arriving and leaving two or three times.
Straight up into the canopy, held for a very long time. This is the film's green, and it wants a flat grey sky rather than sun.
The small dagoba standing in under the tree: brick, lichen, the line where it meets swept earth. Close and static, then macro.
Roots crossing swept ground; wet leaf litter; a rail; an oil lamp; a rag of cloth tied on. Macro, shallow, available light.

Two held frames of equal length, for cutting together: the Buddha images in the image house, and the figures and painted panels of Rama, Sita and Hanuman a few metres away. Neither is given more time, a wider lens or better light than the other.
The lane up on a long lens at eye level, empty: wet tarmac, gate, steps, noticeboard, mist closing the far end.
Rain on the canopy, and water coming off it a drop at a time for the hour after the rain stops. Sound is as important as picture in these.
The payoff: swept ground under the canopy, empty, held far longer than is comfortable, with the light changing on it. This is the closing frame and everything else is built around getting it right.
Late light through the canopy from the west, and then the compound going blue with one lamp in it.
Ambient sound throughout, recorded properly and at length: leaves, water off leaves, a bell, birds, a road a long way below. There is no music in this film.
suggested_location.access: By road, and only by road. The turnoff is reported near the 96th kilometre post on the Nuwara Eliya–Badulla road, about 4 km from Welimada town and about 20 km from Nuwara Eliya, roughly forty minutes' drive from the latter. Commercial listings give the temple as open daily 06:00 to 20:00 with an entrance charge of about 500 rupees for foreign visitors and a published telephone number. It is a small working temple, not a ticketed monument, and filming needs the permission of the incumbent, sought in advance and in person, with the film's intentions stated plainly — in particular the undertaking that no oath, party, witness or ceremony will be filmed. The stupa and the Bodhi pedestal are gazetted protected monuments, so Department of Archaeology permission is likely to be needed for any filming that goes beyond a visitor's camera. The drone is treated as refused: the compound is small, it is in constant devotional use, and there is no frame in this film that a drone could get and a tripod could not.
suggested_location.best_time: Overcast hill mornings, which is the ordinary condition here. The site sits at roughly a thousand metres on a hill plateau where daytime temperatures run in the high teens to mid twenties and nights drop to around twelve; mist in the first hours after dawn is common and is the film's main weather. The wet months give rain on the canopy, water coming off leaves for an hour afterwards, and saturated colour in brick and moss. Hard high sun is the one condition to avoid outright, because it breaks the green under the canopy into blotches. Late afternoon gives the single warm frame. Devotional traffic is likely to be heaviest on poya days and during the Ramayana-trail touring season, and a quiet weekday morning is what this film needs.
suggested_location.research_note: All of this is desk research by web search on 25 September 2026; nothing has been checked on the ground, against a printed edition, or with any Sri Lankan authority. The coordinates are derived: the heritage source gives the site as an Open Location Code, which decodes to 6.9028 N, 80.8850 E, a point about 3 km west of Welimada town on the road in from Nuwara Eliya, consistent with the reported 4 km. They have not been confirmed against a map or a satellite image and should be treated as approximate. The elevation given is likewise approximate and is the town's, not the site's: Welimada is reported at about 1,017 metres, with one source giving about 1,060, and no elevation for the temple itself was found. The meaning of the name, the standing of the place as the proper ground for an oath in settling a dispute, the attribution to Aggabodhi IV, the Bodhi sapling from Anuradhapura, the small dagoba built beneath it, the stupa, the image house, the Mahinda IV slab inscription, the 2002 and 2008 gazette notifications, the 1983 overpainting, the Ramayana identification, the recently added Hindu figures and paintings, and the opening hours, entrance charge and turnoff are all from the sources listed and are single- or double-sourced desk research. The claim that the legal system permits and accepts an oath sworn here, and that one taken here is still valid before village courts or grama sabhas, is repeated almost verbatim across a large number of pages and no primary basis for it was found; it is recorded in what_is_disputed and is the first thing to verify with a Sri Lankan lawyer. The Oaths Ordinance was located but its full text could not be read — the CommonLII PDF returned HTTP 403 — so the statement that it attaches no effect to a named place rests on secondary summary and is not a checked reading of the statute. The colonial-period accommodation of customary oaths at a devale comes from an abstract of a comparative legal history article and the article itself was not read. One conflation was caught and is important: Divurum Bodhi Viharaya at Ampitiya in the Kandy District is a different temple, and the Divurum Gala swearing stone, the Kandyan-kingdom court and the cobra folklore belong to it, not to this site; a general web search on this subject returns them merged, and nothing from that temple is used here. Commons was searched through its search API for Divurumpola, Divurumwela, Nugatalawa, Welimada, Uva Paranagama, Welimada temple and Badulla District Bodhi, and returned nothing of this site or anything near it — the only Welimada-area photographs on Commons are of a waterfall several kilometres away and some electoral maps. A waterfall is not this place and would be a dishonest illustration of a green-lit temple yard, so images is empty rather than filled with a picture of somewhere else. Access, permissions, the incumbent's willingness, the current state of the compound after the recent alterations, whether the oath practice is live today, and drone rules are all unverified; the drone is treated as refused on principle rather than on a checked rule.

unknowns: Whether the legal recognition of an oath sworn here is statutory, customary or merely asserted. Nothing in the film's narration depends on the answer, but the film should not be made without knowing it.
How the oath is actually administered, by whom and how often, and whether the practice is live today or remembered. No first-hand account of the procedure was found in any language searched.
No approach has been made to the incumbent of the temple, and the film cannot be made without their agreement to the terms in what_must_be_real.
The present condition of the compound after the recent addition of figures and paintings, and whether the place still films as a quiet working shrine rather than as a themed attraction.
Whether the temple is quiet enough on an ordinary weekday morning to hold a frame for a minute without anybody walking into it, and whether the film's stillness survives the touring season.
evidence_class_note: Editorial proposal. The location is Claude's suggestion and awaits Chathura's verdict; its supporting detail is desk research and is unverified. No scene or shot is decided here.
